title: Preemptive capacity reservation: Upgrade window optimizer for Dedicated GPU pools
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood Dedicated upgrades of GPU pools frequently interact poorly with the cluster autoscaler. During rolling upgrades we see transient capacity drops because node drains and scale-downs race with eviction and allocation, causing tail latencies and request failures for customers with tight SLOs.

Goal:
Implement a coordinator that reserves short-lived headroom (preemptive capacity tokens) per-pool and orchestrates with the autoscaler and the drain controller to guarantee minimal available serving slots during upgrade waves. This should work across LTS channels: allow different reservation budgets for LTS vs. non-LTS nodes and expose rollout gates so PM/Eng can tune conservatively for customers on stricter SLAs.

Proposed design (summary):
- Preflight stage: compute reservation budget as a function of pool size, historical peak utilization, and current LTS channel. Reservation is expressed as number of GPU slots and duration window (e.g., 5 slots for 30 minutes).
- Reservation token service: lightweight controller that mints tokens and annotates pool objects with reservation metadata. Tokens have TTL and can be extended by the upgrade orchestrator.
- Autoscaler integration: autoscaler must honor reservation annotations by pausing scale-downs below reserved level and treating reserved slots as protected during the reservation window. Also signal to autoscaler to prefer scale-up before evictions when feasible.
- Drain coordination: drain controller consults reservation state to schedule evictions and stagger pod movement while respecting latency SLOs.
- Rollout gates: API flags to enable per-rollout reservation, LTS-sensitive budgets, and a global conservative mode for high-impact customers.
- Observability and runbook: dashboard with reserved vs. active capacity, token lifecycle events, and a rollback path if reservation fails.

Trade-offs and decisions made so far:
- Chose token TTL approach vs. persistent reservation records to limit state churn and make expiry behavior explicit.
- Budget formula will default to max(ceil(0.05 * pool_size), 2) but can be overridden by per-customer configuration and LTS channel. This balances cost vs. safety.
- Avoid hard pre-allocations of instances in cloud; prefer soft reservations honored by the autoscaler to reduce cost and friction for Dedicated billing.

Why this is different from previous work:
Existing tickets focused on drain ordering and evacuation budgeting; this ticket centralizes an explicit preflight reservation primitive that the autoscaler and drain controllers can all consult, making upgrades predictable across a variety of load patterns and LTS channels.
acceptance_criteria: A1: Reservation token controller implemented and unit-tested; tokens have TTL and extend semantics
A2: Autoscaler respects reservation annotations and will not scale below reserved capacity while token is active
A3: Drain controller schedules evictions that avoid violating reserved capacity and provides graceful backoff if headroom is exhausted
A4: End-to-end integration test simulating rolling upgrade + concurrent traffic shows no more than 1% increased 99th latency vs. baseline in canary pool
A5: Monitoring dashboard added (Grafana) showing reserved vs. available slots, token events, and a smoke alert when reservation cannot be fulfilled
A6: Runbook updated with step-by-step for enabling reservation on a rollout, troubleshooting guide, and rollback steps
A7: Canary rollout completed on three low-traffic pools and one high-traffic pool with validation and post-mortem notes
tasks: T1: Write design doc and run quick perf model for budget formula (link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Reservation+Design)
T2: Implement token controller (k8s controller + CRD/annotation approach)
T3: Modify autoscaler to honor reservation annotations and add unit/integration tests
T4: Update drain controller to use reservation state when scheduling evictions
T5: Add Grafana dashboards and alerts (dashboards/upgrade-reservation.json)
T6: Create e2e test harness simulating churn and upgrades (github PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/4123)
T7: Run canary rollout and collect telemetry; iterate on budget formula
T8: Update runbook and ship release notes
comments: 2026-03-01 - Aisha Patel: Initial triage. Observed repeated transient 503s during ENG-40988 test run; spike correlated with aggressive scale-downs. Proposed preflight token idea in design doc draft.

2026-03-03 - Miguel Ortega: Feasibility review complete. Autoscaler change looks minimal if we expose a 'minReservedCapacity' annotation. Need to coordinate with cloud billing to ensure we don't force hard allocations.
2026-03-05 - Design review (PM + SRE): Agreed on TTL/token semantics. PM (Lina Zhou) requested per-customer override and an enterprise conservative mode for Dedicated customers with contractual SLAs.
2026-03-06 - Infra note: Ran capacity model in staging; default budget (5%) holds for 95th percentile load but underestimates for small pools (<10 GPUs). Updated formula to include min=2.
2026-03-09 - Blocker found: cloud quota soft-limits prevented scale-up in one test region. Opened ticket with cloud provider and mitigated by choosing a different canary region. (see ENG-57367)
2026-03-10 - PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2891 - token controller MVP. Waiting for code review from @emma-choi.

2026-03-11 - Code review feedback: Add reconcile backoff and better metrics (tokens minted, tokens expired, tokens extended). Also add integration test that simulates race between scale-down and token expiry.

2026-03-12 - QA: e2e harness run in canary pool 3 completed. Observed safe rollout with reservation enabled; dashboards show reserved slots honored. One regression found: autoscaler metrics emitted an incorrect 'scaledown_skipped' label; tracking fix in ENG-57341
